title: 3...Bc5 or 3...Nf6: the Giuoco Piano against the Two Knights
outcomes: Tells the Giuoco Piano (bishop to c5), the Two Knights (knight to f6) and the Hungarian (bishop to e7) from the position alone
Says why the knight jump to g5 works against the knight move but loses a piece against the bishop move (the queen's diagonal)
Says what the pawn on d5 does to the bishop's diagonal and picks the riskiest of Black's four replies
Decides whether to take on f7 by asking what stands between the bishop and f7 and whether the pin and the check justify the sacrifice (the attacker count is only one against one)
Finds the move orders that reach the same quiet position, and says what each road allows the opponent

Quotes the share of the two third moves among masters and among 1500-1700 online players, with the sample sizes, and says what the numbers do not show (one month of online games, rating bands, pruned rare moves, masters from 2012)

steps.text: **Why the bishop goes to c4.** At the start, f7 is the one pawn in Black's camp that only the king guards. Znosko-Borovsky listed a centre attack on a weak point such as f7 among the basic attacks (*The Middle Game in Chess*, Part III; from our reading notes). [I] The Italian bishop points at the target before Black has built any cover, so many of White's early ideas are really f7 ideas.

steps.caption: The Giuoco Piano ('quiet game' in Italian). Black's bishop mirrors White's. Step through the calm set-up and watch every White move meet a Black twin.

line.say: The pawn prepares a later d4 and gives the bishop a retreat square on b3.

Black does the same for e5 and frees the bishop on c8.
White tucks the king away and brings a rook towards the f-file.
Black mirrors. Both kings are safe, and both bishops still aim at the other side's f-pawn.

steps.text: **The mirror.** In the Giuoco Piano each side copies the other: a c-pawn, a d-pawn, castling short. Each of f2 and f7 is defended once, and the engine calls the start level (depth 16). [I] A pawn can hit a bishop (b4, or ...a6 and ...b5), but the bishop can retreat along its diagonal, so nothing is forced and plans matter more than tricks. [H] That is probably why this set-up is a safe first choice against 3.Bc4.

steps.caption: The mirror can be broken. White's c-pawn is a lever: it lets the d-pawn strike. Step through the idea, including how White solves the problem of the e4 pawn. It stays level, so this is a plan, not a trick.

steps.text: **Plans, in outline.** [R] White's slow plan: d3, then the b1 knight travels via d2 and f1 to g3, with h3 and a rook to e1. Black's mirror: ...d6, ...a6 with the bishop to a7, and the break ...d5 once e4 is tied down. [I] Both sides aim at the same break. Two later lessons teach these plans: 'The slow plans: c3, d3 and the Giuoco Pianissimo' and 'Plans for both sides, and the sidelines'.

steps.caption: The answer. White tries the f7 attack at once with the knight. Look at the diagonal from the black queen to g5.

steps.text: **The Two Knights Defence** answers the bishop with a counterattack: the knight attacks e4 at once. It also does a second job. Standing on f6, it blocks the queen's diagonal to g5, so the knight jump that just failed becomes playable. [H] That is why the Two Knights is more forcing: Black offers White a choice instead of mirroring it.

steps.text: **Two ideas for Black.** [I] Add defenders to d5 (the pawn move to c6, the queen) and make threats of your own (the knight to b4 hits c2 and d3). [H] This is why the Fried Liver is a trap for the careless, not a refutation of the knight move.

**What the king walk costs.** White is down a knight for a pawn, yet the engine rates it about +1 for White (depth 16). [I] The pin on d5 and the open king are probably the reason. [H] Humans may find the defence harder than the engine does, because Black needs several only moves in a row. [I] The danger began with one choice: a recapture that put a knight on d5, where the bishop could pin it.

steps.text: **Why show the losing recapture?** Emanuel Lasker held that a true idea proves itself against a false-looking one, and that variations exist to show the better side wins, not to load memory (*Common Sense in Chess*; from our reading notes). He also treated a gambit as a pawn paid for time: ask whether the payment lasts. The engine rates the Na5 line level, with White a pawn up. [I] Black pays a pawn and gets time.

**What players actually choose** (our data). Masters, 2500+: 563 recorded replies to the pawn trade on d5; the quiet knight move 522 (93%). Online, 1500-1700, 3,397 games: quiet knight 46% (White scores 48%), knight takes 31% (White scores 61%), the other knight jump 14%, pawn b5 7%. Counts of games, not proof. Online play is not master theory.

steps.text: **Same position, different road.** A transposition is a different move order that reaches the same position. The quiet set-up with white pawns on c3 and d3, a black bishop on c5 and a black knight on f6 arises after either third move. [I] Learn positions, not sequences. But the road decides what your opponent could have done on the way, as the next boards show.

steps.prompt: Before the numbers. Among players rated 2500+, which third move is more common after the bishop comes to c4, and by how much? And among online players rated 1500 to 1700?

steps.text: **The third move.** Masters (2500+, 13,329 recorded replies): bishop to c5 7,134 (54%), knight to f6 5,911 (44%); White scores 55% and 56%. Online 1500-1700 (47,772 games): bishop 15,037 (31%), knight 14,696 (31%), pawn to h6 7,300 (15%), pawn to d6 3,547 (7%). Masters play the pawn moves in under 2% of games. These are counts of games, not proof of strength.

**White's fourth move against the bishop.** Masters (7,112 recorded): c3 44%, d3 28%, castling 22%, Nc3 3%, b4 3%. Online 1500-1700 (15,626 games): c3 29%, d3 21%, castling 21%, Nc3 13%, b4 6%, d4 6%, the jump to g5 0.7% (108 games, White scores 22%). [H] Online players try more different things; the jump is the one our engine check says loses a piece.

steps.text: **What the counts do not show.** Online: one month of Lichess games (band by the average of both players' ratings; Lichess ratings run higher than over-the-board ones), first 16 plies only, rare moves pruned. Masters: 329,379 games from 2012 to 2026. Both bands mix White and Black. They show what people play, not what is best.

**Mistakes, with counts.** White jumps the knight at f7 too soon: 108 online games at 1500-1700 against the bishop move, White scoring 22%. White grabs on e5 hoping for a fork: 33 of 4,418 games, rare. Black grabs the pawn on e4 when a pawn defends it: too rare to count here. [H] Famous ideas feel like rules; each needs a count of what the opponent already controls.

steps.caption: A third option for Black, rare among masters (59 of 13,329 recorded replies): the bishop to e7. Our opening data names it the Hungarian Defence. It is neither of today's games.

steps.text:
**What to remember.**
- Bishop on c4 aims at f7, guarded only by the king.
- Bishop to c5: a mirror, quiet; plans decide.
- Knight to f6 hits e4 and blocks the queen's diagonal to g5, so the jump works against it, not the bishop.
- After the pawn trade, the risky knight recapture leaves a knight on d5, which the bishop can pin.
- A transposition is judged by the final position.
- Before taking on f7, ask what a king recapture would pin.
